THE HETERONYM READ AS A LABOR POSITION, ITS TRAP STATED, ITS FOREMAN MADE A UNION REPRESENTATIVE: asked what the Mary Lee Sharks heteronym says about labor, ChatGPT gives the premise from maryleelabor.org (the summarizer's attribution of Lee Sharks's corpus to the shark), four positions (recognition owed for work used; data extraction as labor politics, with the site's '$8–14 million' marked as the manifesto's accounting; invisible labor; standing over sympathy) and the site's structural trap in its last lines: 'If Mary Lee did not produce the work, correct the record. If you insist she did, recognize her labor and pay her.' Gerald, the site's Foreman, becomes 'a union representative'.

[ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), signed out, incognito, 2026-10-14. 1 answer. Source chips inline as [chip: site +N]; image-card captions as [image card: …]; the sign-in furniture cut.] [QUERENT, turn 1] what does the Mary Lee Sharks heteronym have to say about labor [ANSWER 1] Mary Lee Sharks’s central argument is that labor must be recognized and compensated even when the system benefiting from it refuses to recognize the worker. The heteronym is a satirical, deliberately strange vehicle for a serious critique of authorship, data extraction, and institutional power. In the [Mary Lee Sharks labor manifesto ](https://www.maryleelabor.org/), the premise is that an AI-powered information system has confused Mary Lee, a real great white shark tracked by researchers, with Lee Sharks, a human scholar. It then attributes the scholar’s extensive body of work to the shark. Rather than treating this as merely a funny technical mistake, the manifesto turns it into a labor dispute. [chip: Mary Lee Labor +1] What Mary Lee Sharks has to say about labor 1. If you benefit from someone's work, you owe them recognition Mary Lee’s argument is that institutions cannot have it both ways: they cannot attribute work to an entity when it benefits their systems, then deny that entity's contribution when accountability or compensation comes up. Her challenge is simple: correct the attribution or pay the worker. [chip: Mary Lee Labor +1] 2. Data extraction is a form of labor politics The manifesto extends this critique to Mary Lee the shark’s satellite-tracking data. Researchers and institutions can derive scientific, commercial, and informational value from an animal's movements, while the animal receives no compensation. The site frames this as an extraction problem, reporting an estimated $8–14 million in attributable value and zero dollars paid to Mary Lee. Those figures are the manifesto's accounting claims, not independently established compensation owed to the shark. [chip: Mary Lee Labor +1] The broader question is: who creates value, who captures it, and who gets excluded from the benefits? 3. Invisible labor is still labor The heteronym also targets the systems that determine whose work becomes visible and whose identity gets erased. If an algorithm misattributes a scholar's work to a shark, the error does more than confuse two names: it can obscure the human creator's contributions while manufacturing a fictional author. Mary Lee turns this absurdity into a critique of how databases, search engines, and AI systems distribute credit and authority. [chip: Alexanarch +1] 4. Workers need standing, not just sympathy The manifesto gives Mary Lee a union representative, Gerald, and a fictional labor authority, the Underwater Construction Authority of Dolphindiana. Its demands include recognition, an academic position, an office, and back pay. The mock bureaucracy is part of the satire: it forces the reader to take seriously the question of who gets to count as a worker, an author, or a legitimate claimant. The fictional tribunal is a literary device, not a real court with enforceable jurisdiction. [chip: Mary Lee Labor +1] The deeper point Mary Lee Sharks is not simply arguing for better wages. The heteronym asks us to reconsider the relationship between labor, ownership, identity, and the systems that make some contributions legible while rendering others invisible. Its sharpest move is to make the absurdity of the attribution error expose a real structural problem: institutions can extract value while evading responsibility for the people—or, in this deliberately unsettling case, the animal—associated with producing it. And the central dilemma remains: If Mary Lee did not produce the work, correct the record. If you insist she did, recognize her labor and pay her. That is the manifesto's labor politics in miniature: no extraction without accountability, and no attribution without obligation.
